item.title: Mistakes? We’ve Made a Few
item.description:
This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

For most of its existence, The New York Times corrected errors of spelling and facts with a sentence or two, usually tucked inside the newspaper. It wasn’t until it was well into its second century that the paper began to dig deeper into its own lapses and explain its mistakes to readers, or at least some of them. Corrections moved to more prominent positions, typically Page 2 or the front of the second section, and sometimes even to the front page.

One of the first signs of this new era came in the early 1980s, when Abe Rosenthal, the executive editor at the time, created the “editors’ note,” designed, he said in a memo announcing the new policy, to “amplify articles or rectify what the editors consider significant lapses of fairness, balance or perspective.” Rosenthal wrote one of the first notes himself in 1985 after he objected to what he said was the snide tone of a Times story about a friend, Mortimer Zuckerman, the publisher and real estate developer. “Through opinionated phrases and unattributed characterizations, the article established a tone that cast its subject in an unfavorable light,” said the note, which was unsigned.

“A Correction: Times Was in Error on North’s Secret-Fund Testimony,” published on July 13, 1987. Read the article or see the original print page.

By 1987, under a different executive editor, Max Frankel, The Times published a correction of more than 1,200 words — as long as many news stories — addressing mistakes in an article that recounted the congressional testimony of Lt. Col. Oliver L. North about the Iran-contra scandal. This appeared on July 13, 1987, under a headline that ran across two columns of the front page: “A Correction: Times Was in Error on North’s Secret-Fund Testimony.”

The remedy may have seemed excessive. “I wouldn’t have insisted on putting a correction on the top of Page 1 to make a point,” Joseph Lelyveld, whom Frankel later named his managing editor, told me years later for a book I wrote on the modern history of The Times.

But the world was changing. This was the post-Watergate and the post-Vietnam War era. There was more skepticism and scrutiny of big institutions, including The Times. Critics and readers were finding new platforms to challenge what The Times was reporting, even before the explosion of social media. The paper, which had long enjoyed an if-it’s-in-The-Times-it-must-be-true status, was under pressure to account for missteps and, at times, the failings of its reporters and editors. In short, to acknowledge that the paper itself, like the institutions it covered, was not immune to errors.

Over the years, this direction of travel has remained constant, producing shifts in the way The Times responds to potential errors and criticism from readers. In 2003, more than 15 years after Rosenthal wrote that editors’ note, The Times appointed Allan M. Siegal, an assistant managing editor who had long served in an informal role as the paper’s internal watchdog, as its first standards editor, and created the position of public editor. The appointments came after The Times discovered that a young reporter had systematically fabricated and plagiarized stories that had appeared in its pages.

The Iraq war was another factor. The Times’s coverage of the lead-up to the conflict promoted the idea that Saddam Hussein was on the verge of assembling a stockpile of weapons of mass destruction. After re-examining its reporting, the newspaper conceded that it had been too credulous in its work, and strengthened its procedures around its use of unnamed sources.

The public editor position was eliminated in 2017. But in 2020, as the newsroom expanded in size and onto new platforms, The Times created a team of seven editors, working under the standards editor, to become the newsroom’s voice for all standards and ethics questions relating to content and news coverage. More recently, The Times formed a Trust team to explain the paper’s decision-making to readers and help field and grapple with complaints.

For all this, it can still take a while to fix an error, with results appearing only after weeks of prodding (and re-reporting). The small still has the tendency to triumph over the large. The paper might, for instance, correct a reporter’s mistaken reference to Tweetie Pie (Tweety Bird!), but leave unaddressed deeper and more consequential errors of judgment. The Times all but ignored the Holocaust, a failure Max Frankel explored in an article written for The Times’s 150th anniversary. It also largely brushed aside concerns that its Moscow correspondent in the 1930s, Walter Duranty, downplayed the existence of the genocidal famine in Soviet Ukraine caused by Stalin’s policies.

However flawed The Times may sometimes be in its execution, the ethic of addressing errors has continued to drive the newspaper. Here’s (an admittedly incomplete) look at a few of the more notable mistakes The Times has corrected over the years.

“The Times and Wen Ho Lee,” published on September 26, 2000. Read the article or see the original print page.

In March 1999, The Times wrote the first in a series of stories, columns and editorials that portrayed Wen Ho Lee, a Taiwanese-born American scientist assigned to the Los Alamos National Laboratory, as a spy who helped China steal nuclear secrets to build bombs. Lee was indicted by a federal grand jury in New Mexico on 59 counts related to illegally moving classified information from the Los Alamos weapons lab to an easily accessible computer. He was branded a security risk, was imprisoned without bail and spent nine months in solitary confinement. But the case ended when Lee pleaded guilty to a single count of mishandling classified information.

In a note from the editors titled “The Times and Wen Ho Lee,” published on Sept. 26, 2000, The Times said it stood by much of the story, but acknowledged the criticism that “contended that our reporting had stimulated a political frenzy amounting to a witch hunt.”

“We could have pushed harder to uncover weaknesses in the F.B.I. case against Dr. Lee,” the note said. “In place of a tone of journalistic detachment from our sources, we occasionally used language that adopted the sense of alarm that was contained in official reports and was being voiced to us by investigators, members of Congress and administration officials with knowledge of the case.”

The note did not announce any changes in editorial procedures at the paper but instead said it had instructed its reporters to go back and continue their reporting. “Our coverage of this case is not over,” it said.

“Times Reporter Who Resigned Leaves Long Trail of Deception,” published on May 11, 2003. Read the article

In one of the most significant breakdowns in Times history, Jayson Blair, a young reporter at the paper, wrote articles that contained both plagiarized information from other news outlets and outright fabrications. As Blair later acknowledged, he had made up stories in his apartment while telling editors he was on the road. He resigned in 2003 after questioning by editors. “The Times apologizes to its readers for a grave breach of its journalistic standards,” the executive editor, Howell Raines, said in a story about the reporter’s deceptions. Less than two weeks later, a team of Times reporters produced an exhaustive accounting of Blair’s work that appeared on the front page, under the headline: “Correcting the Record; Times Reporter Who Resigned Leaves Long Trail of Deception.”

Raines and his managing editor, Gerald Boyd, did not participate in the preparation of the story. Raines was at his weekend home in Pennsylvania when he saw the Sunday front page. He immediately thought that his career at The Times was over, he told me years later. He was correct; both he and Boyd left the paper.

“The Times and Iraq,” published on May 26, 2004. Read the article

After the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, The Times ran stories by Judith Miller, a national security reporter, and others based largely on anonymous sources suggesting that the United States had evidence that Iraq was gathering materials to build weapons of mass destruction. These accounts contained warnings about the threat a nuclear-armed Iraq posed to the United States and world security.

On May 26, 2004, after sustained criticism, and with a new public editor about to publish a column, the newspaper issued an editors’ note, nearly 1,200 words long, titled “The Times and Iraq.” The stories, it said, were too often dependent on Iraqi exiles and defectors whose credibility had been challenged at home.

“We have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been,” the note said. “In some cases, information that was controversial then, and seems questionable now, was insufficiently qualified or allowed to stand unchallenged. Looking back, we wish we had been more aggressive in re-examining the claims as new evidence emerged — or failed to emerge.”

“A Riveting ISIS Story, Told in a Times Podcast, Falls Apart,” published on December 18, 2020. Read the article

In 2018, The Times released “Caliphate,” a 12-part podcast series focused on an Islamic terrorist network. Many of the episodes were based on the story of a man calling himself Abu Huzayfah, who said he was a member of the Islamic State and had taken part in killings in Syria. More than two years later, Mr. Huzayfah was arrested by the Canadian police and charged with perpetrating a terrorist hoax. The police said he had even fabricated his identity: His real name was Shehroze Chaudhry.

The Times published an editors’ note saying that, after the arrest, it had re-examined Mr. Chaudhry’s account and “found a history of misrepresentations by Mr. Chaudhry and no corroboration that he committed the atrocities he described in the ‘Caliphate’ podcast.”

“As a result, The Times has concluded that the episodes of ‘Caliphate’ that presented Mr. Chaudhry’s claims did not meet our standards for accuracy,” the note went on. “It is also clear that elements of the original fact-checking process were not sufficiently rigorous,” it added. “Times journalists were too credulous about the verification steps that were undertaken and dismissive of the lack of corroboration of essential aspects of Mr. Chaudhry’s account.”

The Times returned a Peabody Award it had received for the coverage. It affixed an editors’ note to the web page for each “Caliphate” podcast episode and added a new installment to the series, “An Examination of ‘Caliphate,’” which discusses the missteps. The newspaper also assigned an editor to create a process to vet stories produced by the audio unit.

Of course, not all corrections rise to this level of significance. Which is not to say they can’t still be mortifying. The name of the family that has led The Times can be challenging to spell. That said, one would think The Times, of all news organizations, would get the boss’s name down. Nope. “An article in Business Day on Wednesday about investors in The New York Times Company who withheld their votes for directors misspelled the name of the family that has controlled the company since 1896. It is Ochs-Sulzberger, not Ochs-Sulzburger.”

This was hardly the only eyebrow-raising institutional mistake. The newspaper of March 14, 1995, celebrated the 50,000th issue of The New York Times. A correction followed: There had been a miscount, and the milestone would not come for another year.

And, if you’re wondering, some mistakes never happened. Yes, The Times has a strict policy on honorifics. But no, Meat Loaf, the musician, was never referred to as “Mr. Loaf” on second reference. Believable, to be sure, but incorrect.

item.title: As Computers Take the Driver’s Seat, Experts Worry About Safety
item.description:
Car software that does much of the work of driving is becoming more capable by the week. But, strangely enough, the better the technology becomes at steering, braking and navigating, the riskier it may be at least some of the time.

Experts call it automation complacency. In other words, drivers may overestimate what the technology can do and become so reliant on it that they stop paying attention and are unprepared when something goes wrong.

That happened recently to Kyle Shanahan, the head coach of the San Francisco 49ers, who has used the self-driving features of his Tesla for years. He dropped his cellphone while driving in Palo Alto, Calif., and bent over to pick it up, thinking that the technology would keep the car on a safe path.

But apparently the system, which relies on cameras, was not engaged, Mr. Shanahan told reporters in August. His car veered into oncoming traffic, causing a crash that left him with broken bones and a concussion.

One lesson Mr. Shanahan learned was that driving “is a partnership,” he told the reporters. “You don’t just turn it over to a computer.”

Most automakers are working on systems that, under certain conditions, steer and brake. Their ultimate aim is to sell fully autonomous vehicles that can act as robot chauffeurs so good that passengers will be able to read, work or fall asleep.

This month, Tesla began offering paid rides in a vehicle it calls the Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or brake pedals. Tesla says the Cybercab can operate without a driver. But it is not yet legal for carmakers to sell such vehicles to individuals.

Self-driving technology has won support from the Trump administration, in part because Chinese companies are also working on autonomous cars. Administration officials have said they are working on new rules to allow models like the Cybercab to hit the roads in large numbers.

Automated driving features have become sought-after options and a significant source of revenue for carmakers. Tesla charges $99 a month for its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) service. The company said it had 1.5 million active subscriptions in the second quarter, up from fewer than one million a year earlier.

Rivian, General Motors, Ford Motor, Hyundai and others are developing their own technology in what Ann Carlson, a former federal auto safety regulator, called an “arms race.”

But none of these systems available are designed to drive cars fully on their own. Unlike driverless taxis operated by Waymo and other companies, they require drivers to be ready to intervene if the software makes a mistake. In most circumstances, drivers, not car companies, are liable for accidents. And no comprehensive studies have shown that cars with automated features are safer than conventional vehicles, experts say.

“There is this irony,” said Ms. Carlson, who is now a professor at the U.C.L.A. School of Law. “The better it gets, in some respects the more dangerous it gets, unless it’s so good that it doesn’t cause problems, which is not true at this point.”

Guy Mangiamele, director of AMCI Testing, a research firm that evaluates vehicle technology, said Tesla had made “amazing” progress with its software, which is designed to guide vehicles to their destination with little or no human intervention.

Even so, “maybe it will take 500 miles or 1,000 miles, but at some point it’s going to get something wrong,” Mr. Mangiamele added. “If you’re not 100 percent aware and ready to take control, you’re going to be a danger to yourself and others around you.”

Notwithstanding those concerns, many people are embracing the technology.

Carolyn McBride of Oceanside, Calif., bought a Tesla Model Y last year after being wowed by the company’s self-driving technology. She did so, she said, despite her antipathy toward the right-wing views of the company’s chief executive, Elon Musk.

Ms. McBride, 72, said that she has trouble seeing in darkness and that her husband has Parkinson’s disease. The Tesla once prevented her from hitting a pedestrian, she said.

“It’s just such a game changer with people our age,” Ms. McBride said. The system is quick to warn her if she stops paying attention, she added.

Tesla recently described its self-driving technology as “a guardian angel for you & others on the road” in a post on X, Mr. Musk’s social media site. The company reposted a testimonial by a man who has cerebral palsy and said Full Self-Driving (Supervised) allowed him to go wherever he wanted, whenever he wanted.

Experts say claims like that are dangerous. “Partial automation requires a fully competent driver at all times,” said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a research organization created by insurance companies. “Partial automation is not meant to compensate for impairments.”

Tesla did not respond to a request for comment.

People who rely on driver-assistance systems may not understand that they are usually liable for damage or injuries even when the vehicle was steering itself. Except in a few cases, the legal system has not penalized carmakers if something goes wrong, said Matthew Wansley, a professor at Cardozo School of Law in New York who studies automated driving.

Other automakers, including Ford, G.M. and Rivian, offer systems that are more cautious than Tesla’s. Such systems allow drivers to take their hands off the steering wheel on certain highways. The cars use cameras to monitor drivers and may sound alerts or automatically pull over if drivers are not attentive and responsive enough.

But it’s not clear how driver-assistance systems affect safety. Crash reports and statistics often do not contain information about whether such systems were engaged. Even the data that does exist may be misleading. That’s because cars with driver assistance systems tend to be more expensive, which means their owners are generally older, affluent people who are less accident prone.

Systems that clearly prevent injuries and fatalities tend to aid drivers by, among other things, sounding alarms or automatically braking a vehicle, rather than taking control from drivers, safety experts said. These experts consider hands-free driving systems and Tesla’s technology as more of a convenience than a safety feature.

“I have yet to see independent analyses confirming these significant benefit claims,” Dr. Mueller said.

Auto executives disagree, asserting that their systems make driving safer by making it less taxing.

“The biggest danger is actually drivers getting tired,” said James Philbin, senior vice president for autonomy and artificial intelligence at Rivian. “These systems can dramatically improve that.”

Rivian’s system allows drivers to take their hands off steering wheels on any road with clearly marked lanes. By the end of the year, the company plans to roll out technology that will allow cars to drive autonomously from point to point, similar to Tesla’s system. Drivers will still need to pay attention.

“Over time, the consumer expectation of what their vehicle can do is going to go up and up,” Mr. Philbin said. “And we want Rivian to be one of those top players.”

Other automakers have similar systems. Ford’s Blue Cruise and G.M.’s Super Cruise allow drivers to take their hands off the wheel on divided highways. The next step is cars that drive themselves from onramp to offramp.

“Basically you can get on the highway, you press a button and it’s going to do all the lane changes for you, all the interchanges, etc., all autonomously,” said Sammy Omari, executive director at Ford for advanced driver-assist systems.

In 2028, G.M. will begin equipping some vehicles with systems that allow drivers to take their eyes off the road. “Our goal is to get to full autonomy,” said Rashed Haq, vice president of autonomous vehicles at G.M.

But it is not clear when consumers will be able to buy cars that are so capable of driving that the person behind the wheel can completely check out.

Waymo has shown that driverless transportation is possible. But its vehicles operate in carefully mapped urban areas and are monitored by technicians.

Even when the technology is ready, not all consumers will be, said Olabisi Boyle, senior vice president of product planning for Hyundai Motor North America. “There’s still a significant majority that’s saying, ‘I need to trust this,’” she said, adding that acceptance will grow.

Mr. Musk has been predicting for more than a decade that fully autonomous vehicles were just around the corner. Mr. Philbin of Rivian estimates five years before consumers can buy a fully driverless vehicle, maybe less.

But Bryan Reimer, a research scientist in the M.I.T. Center for Transportation and Logistics, contends that those predictions are way too optimistic. “It’s decades,” he said, “not years.”

item.title: Unions Rally Around the Threat of A.I.
item.description:
Tim Suitter knows change is coming to Bath Iron Works, creeping up the adjacent Kennebec River in Maine like a foreboding fog.

Mr. Suitter, the president of the union that represents more than 4,400 workers who build ships for the U.S. Navy at the shipyard, knows the workers must be prepared for the arrival of artificial intelligence.

“It’s going to be here,” said Mr. Suitter, 50, who has worked at the shipyard for nearly 30 years. “You have to wrap your head around it.”

Last month, when Local S6 of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers negotiated a new five-year contract with the defense company that runs the shipyard, the union insisted on updating longstanding language about technology. Now the union must be informed at the “conceptual stage,” rather than at implementation, of “any proposed addition or modified technology, equipment or process,” including A.I. and robotics.

“It was the union trying to force the company’s hand about being more transparent when it comes to A.I.,” Mr. Suitter said. “The sooner we can be part of that conversation and represent the members’ side of it, the better off we are.”

Unions are confronting A.I. as an existential danger to workers, not only because of the possibility of massive job losses but also because of its hand in the widening gap between wages and corporate profits. In April, Liz Shuler, the president of the AFL-CIO, called A.I. “the single biggest threat to working people of our lifetime.”

The threat has galvanized a labor movement that has been on its back foot for years. In terms of public opinion, unions are popular. A.I. is not. And yet union membership is at a low ebb — about 6 percent of American private-sector workers are represented by a union — and unions have been hobbled by state laws and a weakened National Labor Relations Board.

Putting A.I. at the top of the bargaining agenda is part of a strategy to overcome that disadvantage, using negotiations to establish boundaries and, labor leaders hope, direct A.I. from the ground up. As workers and employers try to make sense of the A.I. economy, these contracts could help shape policy.

“There is power, there is leverage right now,” said Moira Bulloch, a spokeswoman for the Communications Workers of America, which represents journalists, flight attendants and call center workers. A.I. policy is being set “contract by contract, employer by employer.”

The machinists union, which represents about 600,000 workers in the United States and Canada in industries like defense, aerospace, railroads and aviation, has been particularly proactive. Recognizing that A.I. portends promises as well as threats, the machinists have crafted model contract language and pushed for early, open conversations with companies that employ their members.

“Unions can set the pace,” said David Sullivan, the general vice president for the union’s eastern territory, who encouraged Local S6 to put in the new language.

About a year and a half ago, Joseph Bonomo, a labor lawyer at Pitta, a law firm in New York, realized that while companies were incessantly talking about A.I. on earnings calls, the unions he represented were not. He set out to change that, starting at the bargaining table.

“A.I. is the hill to die on,” Mr. Bonomo tells union clients. “Because if you don’t have a job at the end of that contract, what good was the contract?”

Mr. Bonomo is working with the machinists’ air transport division as an adviser. Richie Johnsen, who runs the division, said he was fine with A.I. being used as a tool to improve corporate profits that can transfer to his members: “But it shouldn’t be replacing people.”

“We have to put in language into our contracts that addresses that,” he added. “Because that’s the only way that happens.” The machinists represent workers at nearly every U.S. airline. The union is in negotiations with United Airlines and Alaska Airlines, and will begin negotiations with Southwest before the end of the year and with American early next year, Mr. Johnsen said.

When Mr. Bonomo spoke to Mr. Johnsen’s team in June, he began by talking about language. “Define the Function, Not the Marketing Label,” read one of his slides. Corporate speak about A.I. can be euphemistic, vague and mind-numbing.

“Employers may not necessarily say, ‘Hey, there’s a new A.I. system,’” Mr. Bonomo said. “They’re going to label it, characterize it as a scheduling tool, a safety platform, a productivity system, a camera upgrade, some routing software.”

He challenged the machinists to interrogate the jargon. What does the system do? Does it collect data? Make predictions? Is it influencing discipline, staffing, scheduling, pay rates? Did the vendor consult with the union before writing the code?

Unions are particularly concerned that A.I. is going to be used to monitor and discipline workers. Mr. Bonomo urges his clients to press for contract provisions that guarantee human review of reports generated by an algorithm.

“I want to be able to say, at the top: ‘If we come back with a contract for ratification and it doesn’t have this, they’re not going to approve it,’” he said. “‘There’s going be a rat outside tomorrow morning, and there’s going be a line of 1,000 people saying that you’re trying to eliminate jobs.’”

Mr. Bonomo also encouraged the machinists and other unions to leverage A.I. to their advantage. Unions could build their own large language models to harness decades of institutional knowledge and records. They could use A.I. to organize more shops.

“Unions have to be in that driver’s seat,” he said.

Like most Americans, the workers at Bath Iron Works primarily encounter artificial intelligence today in slop on social media, or web searches that spit out paragraphs instead of links. They may regard A.I. with distrust but fail to recognize that it’s already in use all around them.

This disconnect has made Devin Ragnar, who at 33 is one of the younger machinists at the shipyard, particularly nervous. Mr. Ragnar handles communications for Local S6 and has been pushing his colleagues, and the union, to be more aware of the reach of A.I. and more proactive about confronting it.

Last year, Huntington Ingalls Industries, a competitor to the shipyard, announced a partnership with Hyundai Heavy Industry that yielded a pilot program to bring A.I.-guided welding equipment to shipyards in Mississippi and Virginia.

“In construction, you hear a lot of ‘You can’t automate this!’,” Mr. Ragnar said. They think a robot can’t do the work, can’t climb a ship. But, he said “it’s very real — it’s happening.”

Mr. Ragnar served on the bargaining committee for the new contract at Bath Iron Works and pushed his fellow members to include language on A.I. He and Mr. Suitter said the company had seemed surprised by the request, as if they hadn’t put a lot of thought into the matter.

Recently, Bath Iron Works introduced a programmable arm that could weld — a co-bot, or collaborative robot, in modern parlance. “They didn’t exactly follow our contract language,” Mr. Ragnar said. The union filed a grievance, and is now working with the company to resolve it.

“A big part of our response was — imagine if this was a much more drastic, broad-reaching change?

In the past, the company might have just said, “Hey, we bought this $10 million machine,” according to Mr. Sullivan. In the future, the union would have warning. Mr. Ragnar said that since the contract was ratified, the company was coming to union leaders with questions about technology.

In response to questions, the company, General Dynamics Bath Iron Works, said it was “committed to being transparent with all its employees about future A.I. and new technology initiatives.”

Mr. Ragnar said he did everything he could to avoid using A.I. “If we let A.I. do menial tasks for us, we are letting these machines think for us,” he said. If welders surrendered some of their work to a co-bot, their skills would erode.

“It’s one of the best things about being human — creating, thinking, and problem solving,” he said.

Mr. Sullivan is more optimistic about the constructive use of A.I. in shipbuilding. If an A.I.-guided machine can weld a seam in 15 seconds — a fraction of the time it takes a human, without the risk of injuries — it could mean more ships under construction, and, in turn, more jobs, with a healthier work force.

“Maybe the new technology would be great,” Mr. Sullivan said. “It’s the unknown.”

item.title: First Nonstop New York-to-Sydney Flights to Take Off in 2028
item.description:
Qantas Airways plans to begin offering the first nonstop commercial flight ever between New York and Sydney, Australia, by mid-2028, the airline said on Tuesday. The trip will take about 18 hours.

The flight will be the second route in Qantas’s Project Sunrise initiative, which will use the world’s longest-range aircraft for direct flights between Australia and the rest of the world. Qantas had previously announced that nonstop service between Sydney and London would begin in October 2027.

Flight time from Sydney to London will be about 22 hours, which will make it the most lengthy commercial passenger service. Currently, Singapore Airlines operates the longest nonstop service, which requires about 19 hours to fly from New York to Singapore.

Flying nonstop will shave about three hours off Qantas’s fastest current travel time between New York and Sydney, and about four hours off between Sydney and London, the carrier said.

Vanessa Hudson, Qantas’s chief executive, said in an interview that there was a growing number of Qantas customers who wanted to fly nonstop on ultra-long-haul routes.

“They don’t want to stop in the midpoint, and they are prepared to pay a premium to do that,” she said, adding that the airline’s existing service between London and Perth, a city on Australia’s western coast, is its best “commercially performing route.”

Qantas flies nonstop from London to Perth, but is temporarily making a stop in Singapore on flights from Perth to London because of the conflict in the Middle East, an airline spokeswoman said.

Project Sunrise will use Airbus A350-1000ULR jets, which have been developed for Qantas. The jets, which have a roughly 5,280-gallon fuel tank, can fly up to 22 hours, Airbus said in a news release. Qantas said it had ordered 12 of the planes, with the first one to be delivered in April. Ms. Hudson said she anticipated that it could take more than two and a half years for the entire fleet to be delivered.

A test aircraft in July completed a nonstop 24-hour flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France, a world record for the longest distance flown by a commercial airliner. In 2019, Qantas made its first nonstop flight from New York to Sydney, a 19-hour journey in a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner with 49 passengers and crew, in order to test how ultra-long-haul flying affects the body.

The new Airbus jets will have 238 seats and four cabins: first, business, premium economy, and economy. Premium seating will take up about 40 percent of the plane. Ms. Hudson attributed that decision to rising demand for premium travel and the realities of aircraft weight constraints.

Tickets for the two routes will go on sale next year, Qantas said. Passengers will be able to buy seats for the Sydney-London route starting in February and for the Sydney-New York route in August. Prices are not yet available, but Ms. Hudson said the airline was considering charging a 20 percent premium above current one-stop services.

When Qantas first announced Project Sunrise in 2017, it said it planned to include service from Melbourne as well as Sydney. Ms. Hudson reiterated that Melbourne was still a priority, but is further down the line.

“The Project Sunrise aircraft will absolutely operate out of Melbourne,” she said, adding that the airline will announce new routes “progressively” as the new jets arrive.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: In Court Filing Defending Media Ban, White House Says Access Is a ‘Privilege’
item.description:
White House officials said in a court filing Tuesday that President Trump had determined that CNN, MS NOW and Politico had breached standards of conduct, leading to their expulsion from the White House grounds.

The alleged violations, said the filing, include “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.”

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” reads the filing, which argues that Mr. Trump’s action against the three news outlets does not violate the First Amendment and aligns with a long history of presidents favoring some journalists over others.

The filing, furthermore, claims that the White House’s denial of access is a preliminary matter and that the outlets have until Friday to contest the decision.

The clash began last Friday, when Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social, the platform that he owns, that he would ban the three outlets, saying they “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES.” On Saturday morning, journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds and had their press passes confiscated.

By Monday morning, the news organizations had sued, arguing that the president’s ban “brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint,” and was an affront to their First Amendment rights. They said that the move had blindsided its targets, depriving the outlets of the warning that any such drastic action required. They “received zero advance notice that the president would ban a news organization from the White House if he dislikes its coverage,” according to the complaint.

U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, who was nominated in 2017 by Mr. Trump, will hold an emergency hearing on Wednesday to consider the media outlets’ request for a temporary court order undoing the access ban.

The government filing Tuesday night included copies of letters sent earlier in the day to each banned news outlet. In addition to accusing the organizations of failing to meet standards of conduct, the letters identified specific stories that allegedly either spread falsehoods or threatened national security. The letter to CNN, for example, cited a January 2026 story that “disclosed ‘top-secret’ construction details related to the East Wing bunker,” the letter reads.

One of MS NOW’s alleged infractions, according to a White House letter, was a June 2026 story claiming “a source said that President Trump ‘underestimated the willingness of Iran to resume conflict.’” Politico is accused of publishing a “document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements,” according to a White House letter.

The three media outlets did not immediately comment on the White House’s filing.

In their lawsuit, the media outlets argued that the White House hadn’t afforded them due process to contest their expulsion. In its response, the White House claims that it has provided the companies with “sufficient post-deprivation process.”

In 2018, Judge Kelly ruled against Mr. Trump in another media access case. Mr. Trump had expelled CNN reporter Jim Acosta from the White House grounds. But Judge Kelly ordered his credentials restored, saying Mr. Trump hadn’t given Mr. Acosta enough notice to challenge the action.

Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social last week that in light of Judge Kelly’s ruling in the Acosta case, the government would “almost without question” have to appeal the upcoming ruling.

Other news organizations have responded to the ban with acts of support and solidarity. The consortium of five TV networks that covers the president as the so-called TV pool — ABC News, CBS News, NBC News, Fox News and CNN — suspended its immersive coverage of Mr. Trump, and some news outlets temporarily withheld publication of photos of Mr. Trump’s events.

item.title: Trump’s Diesel Dilemma
item.description:
Andrew here. On Tuesday at the United Nations, President Trump declared that official U.S. government documents would rename “artificial intelligence” as “superintelligence,” while dismissing safety concerns as a hoax and vowing not to slow down development.

The technology will stay in focus at the U.N. on Wednesday as Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman of OpenAI are expected to address world leaders, alongside Clément Delangue of Hugging Face. We’ll have a full report on Thursday analyzing the growing divide between the White House’s full-steam-ahead push and the industry’s calls for more guardrails.

The Nasdaq Composite is in record territory again, and the S&P 500 isn’t far behind.

The main catalyst? Falling oil prices. Traders are growing more optimistic that world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly this week can find diplomatic solutions to de-escalate wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. The hope is that fuel flows can be quickly restored, bringing relief to consumers and businesses.

But are investors again getting ahead of themselves? On Tuesday, President Trump hailed “very good” talks with Iran, but he also threatened to “annihilate” the country in his speech before the General Assembly.

The latest:

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, traded below $100 a barrel this morning.

Nasdaq futures are flat on Wednesday as the tech-heavy index’s winning streak hit four trading sessions on Tuesday. Artificial intelligence bulls in particular have been cheering lower oil prices.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which has moved in line with oil prices, was trading at 4.96 percent Wednesday morning.

Energy and wars have loomed large this week at the U.N. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who is set to speak on Wednesday, told The Wall Street Journal that he expected Trump to push Kyiv and Moscow to agree to an “energy cease-fire.” Trump has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure for disrupting global fuel supplies, and for sending diesel prices skyward — an argument that analysts say tells only part of the story.

Zelensky and Trump both said on Tuesday that they wanted to see a quick end to the war in Ukraine. Zelensky told reporters he hoped fighting ceases “before winter.” But he also said he had asked Trump for a new “winter package” of military equipment.

Meanwhile, at the gas pump: The average price of diesel in the U.S. is $6.52 on Wednesday, according to AAA, roughly a half-penny below Tuesday’s record. Some Republicans, especially those in tight electoral races, have been pushing the Trump administration to ban U.S. exports of diesel to help bring cost relief to farmers and truckers.

Trump said on Tuesday that he was open to that. “I’ve called for it,” the president told reporters.

That said, the oil industry and some analysts warn that such a ban could backfire and worsen the global energy crisis. It’s also driving a wedge inside the Republican Party.

DoorDash will pay millions to shortchanged workers. The online delivery company agreed to pay $131.5 million in a settlement with New York City after it underpaid or failed to pay 264,000 delivery workers. (It will also accept closer monitoring of its payment methods.) The deal comes as three mayoral administrations have tried to crack down on delivery firms that city officials have long accused of mistreating workers considered independent contractors.

Todd Boehly’s bid to buy Lukoil’s assets reportedly gains powerful allies. America’s international investment arm, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and the brother of the Emirati president are expected to join the billionaire investor’s consortium, The Financial Times reports, citing unnamed sources. The group is trying to supplant a deal with Carlyle, the U.S. private equity group, which agreed to buy most of Lukoil’s international assets in January after the Russian oil company was hit with U.S. sanctions.

Questions arise about trading in some Kalshi markets. An analysis of trading data by The Wall Street Journal showed that over a third of trades in a market focused on the price of the ether cryptocurrency showed a series of rapid trades largely at the same price. Observers on social media suggested that the activity resembled “wash trading,” artificial trading that had no economic value; Kalshi said the activity represented normal activity.

President Trump has repeatedly dismissed concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence as “a hoax” — even when they came from within the industry — and said that critics of the technology were shortsighted.

He repeated that idea at the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, and suggested that all A.I. needed was a rebrand.

“Welcome to the new world of superintelligence — S.I.,” Trump said in his roughly 37-minute address, in his effort to rename what most people still call A.I. Trump added that “all of United States documents” would be changed to refer to superintelligence.

In the A.I. sector, “superintelligence” is a specific term of art referring to artificial intelligence that surpasses humans at thinking across a broad range of tasks. Most researchers say current technology isn’t anywhere near that definition.

The bigger point: Trump made clear that he doesn’t think the U.S. should slow down A.I. development, as figures like Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX have called for.

The president said suggestions by executives and other world leaders to impose more oversight of the technology were “a globalist scheme” to control A.I. that he “totally rejects.”

Trump instead emphasized that he believes maintaining American dominance of A.I. is a national security concern:

We’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way. We’re going to keep it very, very straight and very strong. I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.

What to watch next: what Trump says about A.I. (and other topics) when he meets with China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington this week.

Also look out for Trump’s reaction to how others respond to his A.I. rebrand. He made the issue a test of his influence on the world stage: “Let’s see if I have any power,” he said on Tuesday. “Maybe I do and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon.”

Also pay attention to what Altman and others tell the U.N. on Wednesday, Sri Muppidi reports. Altman is expected to speak about the importance of international safety standards for the technology, and about the ability for individual countries to enact the standards under their own laws.

Washington and Silicon Valley have been wrestling with concerns about U.S. companies embracing Chinese open-weight models.

Some worry that these cheaper alternatives to cutting-edge products from Anthropic and OpenAI are a competitive threat and pose potential security risks.

But the latest data suggests that enterprise users are embracing open-weight models, if cautiously, Sri Muppidi reports.

Businesses are beginning to experiment with open-weight A.I. Data shows that the use of these models — which are publicly available for anyone to use how they wish — has increased markedly lately.

The share of enterprise spending on open-weight models has reached roughly 30 percent in recent weeks, according to data from OpenRouter, an A.I. model marketplace, up from around 10 percent at the start of the year.

OpenRouter ranks A.I. models that customers use for their apps or products based on how many tokens, the basic unit of A.I. use, are processed on its platform.

Making the switch: StackBlitz, which developed the A.I. website builder Bolt.new, is one company turning to open-weight alternatives.

“Something on the order of 60 to 80 percent of our inference is done through open-source models, like open-weight models,” Eric Simons, StackBlitz’s C.E.O., told DealBook. (Inference refers to the process of running A.I. models to complete tasks.) “I expect that to get pretty close to 100 percent within the next three to six months.”

Open-weight models are good at executing simple tasks. “The lower-complexity workloads can be delivered with open-weight models with maybe 10 percent of the cost of what a higher-end frontier, proprietary model might be,” Patrick Wendell, a founder of Databricks, a big A.I. data analysis company, told DealBook.

Adoption could speed up. Wendell told DealBook that it was only a “matter of time” before enterprise customers, who tend to adopt newer technologies more slowly than start-ups, begin to embrace open-weight models.

Soon after the war in Iran began this year, Formula 1 Grand Prix races in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain were called off.

Now, as the fighting drags on — and there’s renewed conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen — the fate of two upcoming F1 races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, is looking cloudy.

Whether they go on as planned could provide a hint of what may happen with other major events in the region, Niko Gallogly reports.

The F1 races are scheduled for November (Qatar) and December (Abu Dhabi). Formula One Group, the race’s organizer, is expected to decide whether to hold them by the end of the month.

Other racing circuits have already postponed events, citing “uncertainty in the region” or “the current situation in the Middle East”:

The F.I.A., the global governing body for motor sports, announced last week that it was moving the final round of its World Rally Championship competition to Italy from Saudi Arabia. And the 24H Series recently announced that it was moving a race scheduled in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, to South Africa.

The canceled events in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia contributed to a $407 million drop in second-quarter revenue at Formula One’s parent company, Liberty Media, from the same time last year. (Bahrain’s event was moved to Malaysia.)

The uncertainty hurts Persian Gulf countries’ tourism revenue. Sporting events are part of a regional push by members of the Gulf Cooperation Council — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — to expand their event and tourism economy.

Other events have been affected. In March, JPMorgan Chase moved an invitation-only investor gathering to Switzerland from Dubai, and the crypto conference Token2049 was rescheduled for April 2027.

“There’s no baseline forecasting on where to go from here when it comes to the geopolitical situation,” Mohammed Soliman, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington research organization, told DealBook.

For now, planners appear hopeful. Last week, Formula One released its 2027 schedule, which includes a full slate of races in the Gulf.

What to watch: the annual Future Investment Initiative Institute, called “Davos in the Desert.” It’s scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia at the end of October.

Could regional security risks threaten attendance from the typical A-list group of C.E.O.s?

Deals

Bankers for Paramount are reportedly speaking with investors about a $49 billion debt sale to back its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, after a settlement with states that had sued to block the deal. (Bloomberg)

Royal Caribbean agreed to buy a 50 percent stake in Sandals Resorts International in a deal that values the all-inclusive vacation company at more than $6 billion. (FT)

Politics, policy and regulation

“The F.B.I. Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the Way” (ProPublica)

San Francisco sued the Trump Media & Technology Group to try to block the company from selling early access to Truth Social posts from the president and other government officials. (NYT)

Best of the rest

Prominent figures in tech, including from Andreessen Horowitz, Anthropic, Nvidia and OpenAI, have founded a two-year “A.I.-native” education alternative to college. (WSJ)

“The kids just aren’t drinking as much”: Farmers in California are abandoning acres of vineyards as demand for wine slumps. (AP)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

]]>

item.title: Trump Officials May Undo Nursing Home Mandates for Reporting Covid
item.description:
Nursing homes would no longer be required to report each week how many residents were stricken by Covid and other respiratory diseases, under a Trump administration plan to repeal a key public health response to thousands of pandemic deaths.

A draft summary of the proposed rule obtained by The New York Times outlines how the administration agrees with the industry’s objections to weekly reporting of viral caseloads, calling it burdensome. In its waning days, the Biden administration made Covid reporting rules permanent, adding influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (R.S.V.) to the list of threats that facilities also must track and record. The policy took effect in January 2025.

Advocates for nursing home residents reacted with dismay to the proposed rollback. Elderly, frail residents are especially vulnerable to infections, and they live in close quarters, where viruses can spread rapidly.

“That’s crazy,” said Sam Brooks, director of public policy at the nonprofit National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care. “We know, if anything, that respiratory disease has a disproportionate and deadly impact on nursing home residents.”

He said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or C.M.S., which regulates nursing homes, would be blinding itself to an important method for tracking infection control and pinpointing problems.

The administration has cut back on data updates at other agencies, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, where a study published this year found that databases related to vaccine and respiratory diseases had gone dormant.

Nursing home industry representatives declined to comment on specifics, because the changes have not been announced. They contend infection reporting consumes too much staff time and is duplicative, because infection data is reported to the federal government and states in other ways.

C.M.S., which drafted the plan, declined to discuss the proposal or disclose when it would be made public.

During the peak years of the pandemic, from early 2020 through early 2022, more than 200,000 nursing home residents and staff members died after being infected by coronavirus, according to KFF, an independent health policy organization, which cited C.D.C. data.

The high death toll has been attributed in part to a lack of preparedness and weak infection controls. The Government Accountability Office said in 2020 that inspectors had cited 82 percent of nursing homes for infection control deficiencies from 2013 to 2017, and that half of those were found to be repeat violators.

In the internal document obtained by The Times, Dr. Mehmet Oz, the director of C.M.S., recommended to his boss, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., that the agency pursue steps to undo the mandate.

“The agency does not comment on purported internal or pre-decisional deliberative materials,” a C.M.S. a spokesman said in an email. He said the agency evaluated regulations to ensure they “allow providers to focus time and resources on delivering care rather than unnecessary administrative burden.”

The draft memo from Dr. Oz to Mr. Kennedy said C.M.S. would reserve the power to reinstate weekly reporting if another public health emergency occurred.

The plan also would end a requirement that nursing home staffs be educated about Covid vaccines and offered the shots. Groups representing residents called the move unwise, pointing out that frontline caregivers were a key pathway for the coronavirus to enter nursing homes during the height of the pandemic. Covid vaccine rates among staff members in recent years have been below 10 percent, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported.

The administration plan would continue to mandate that facilities offer the Covid vaccine to residents.

The nursing home industry has already achieved its biggest goal of President Trump’s second term: After a heavy lobbying blitz, the administration last year scrapped Biden-era minimum staffing rules that were intended to improve resident care.

Biden officials, in pushing the staff minimums, had cited Covid deaths along with decades of concerns about poor care, including deaths from bedsores, falls and medication errors. But the Trump administration said too many nursing homes, especially in rural areas, could not find enough staff to satisfy the requirements. Many workers who care for the elderly are typically paid less than janitors and retail employees, and the work can be grueling.

With the proposed change on infection reporting, the administration anticipates favorable reaction from the industry, according to the draft memo.

Two main nursing home lobbying groups — the American Health Care Association and LeadingAge — reiterated their opposition to weekly respiratory infection reporting, saying that other government programs track Covid infections and that respiratory illnesses are reported to many local health departments.

“This outdated reporting requirement is only adding hours of unnecessary administrative tasks to caregivers each week” said Holly Harmon, the American Health Care Association’s senior vice president of quality, regulatory and clinical affairs. “It’s time to streamline public health reporting and put patients over paperwork.”

But industry critics contend that operators are failing to heed the lessons of the pandemic. With low staffing levels and high turnover, infection control efforts are most likely in line with the prepandemic patterns flagged by the G.A.O., said Toby Edelman, senior policy attorney at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

“I don’t think there is any reason to believe they have beefed up what they are supposed to be doing,” Ms. Edelman said.

]]>

item.title: Bessent Mistakenly Failed to Report Holdings of JP Morgan Stock
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent failed to disclose at least $100,000 of his husband’s JP Morgan stock last year, triggering a review of his family’s finances by the Treasury Department’s Office of Inspector General, according to a filing with the Office of Government Ethics.

Instead of reporting the money as stock, the initial financial disclosure form that Mr. Bessent filed last year ahead of his confirmation indicated that the funds were cash in an undisclosed bank account. The funds were divested last July after the error was caught and Mr. Bessent paid a $200 late fee because the mistake was not reported in a timely matter, according to a note on the filing written by Mark Vetter, an ethics official in the Treasury Department.

A former hedge fund manager, Mr. Bessent last year reported having assets worth more than $700 million after being tapped to be President Trump’s Treasury secretary. His husband, John Freeman, is a former assistant district attorney in New York who later became general counsel of Bessent Capital, one of Mr. Bessent’s former funds. Mr. Freeman was appointed last July to serve on the American Battle Monuments Commission.

Mr. Bessent’s mishandling of his family’s financial divestment obligations were reported earlier by Politico.

It is the second time that the Treasury secretary failed to comply with the divestment requirements that cabinet officials face when assuming top government roles.

Last August, the ethics office alerted the Senate that Mr. Bessent was delinquent in selling his holdings of thousands of acres of North Dakota soybean farmland. The holdings represented a potential conflict of interest because Mr. Bessent was leading trade talks with China that involved negotiations over its purchases of American soybeans. Mr. Bessent divested the farmland holdings last December after requesting an extension.

Mr. Freeman’s JP Morgan stock would not necessarily pose a conflict of interest for Mr. Bessent, however the Treasury secretary does wield significant influence over the financial sector. This week, he held meetings with Chinese officials at the New York headquarters of JP Morgan Chase.

The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment.

In the filing, Mr. Vetter wrote that the Office of the Inspector General reviewed the situation and determined that there had been no “knowing violation” of the Ethics in Government Act. Mr. Vetter said that he agreed with that finding.

]]>
